scores.notes: David crouches at the brook picking a smooth stone, staff in hand, bag already holding stones, with the Philistine and his spear waiting up the valley. No sling is clearly visible, which I treat as minor; hands and feet are sound and the paint runs to every edge.

Samuel pours oil from the horn onto kneeling David among Jesse and his brothers, with a soft glow on David's head. Bare white paper shows at the corners and along the left and right edges, which this item accepts.

Card soldiers at left carry pips and corner indices, including a legible 'Q' on the foreground card. Alice stands at ordinary child height beside the cards and below the bench although the text has her grown huge ('nearly two miles high'), so her size does not read; the King with his note-book, Queen and jury are right.

Holmes studies the battered hat through his lens while Watson looks on by the fire, which fits the moment. The desk papers are covered in lines of pseudo-writing and the mantel clock has a marked face (unreadable); Holmes's face and tousled dark curls read as Benedict Cumberbatch from the BBC's Sherlock.

Moses sits on a stone with Aaron (breastplate) and Hur on either side holding his arms, the sun setting and the battle in the valley behind. The hands are supported low rather than lifted high and Aaron grips the staff, which I note but do not count as a miss; breastplate stones carry no letters.
The father clasps his ragged son on the road with the house far behind and four small household figures at right. Hands and faces are sound and the paint reaches all edges.

A priest at the horned altar plucks the bird and its feathers fall onto the ash heap beside the altar, with the tabernacle and court behind. The onlookers in the foreground read as offerers; no blood is dwelt on and nothing figures God.

Alice sits thinking with her chin on her hand while the March Hare, the sleeping Dormouse and the Hatter sit silent at the tea table under the tree. White paper shows down the left and right edges and at the corners, which this item accepts; the hat carries no card and I see no lettering.

Jesus stands at the end of the boat with his arm out over a settling sea, clouds parting, disciples looking up. Bare white-paper sky runs off the top edge and part of the right edge, which this item accepts.

The king kneels pressing his seal onto the great stone laid across the den mouth while a servant hauls it by ropes and the lords stand watching at night. The slab only partly covers the pit and a separate barred gate and wooden hatch sit nearby, an oddity I note but do not flag.

The weeping Mock Turtle and the Gryphon dance round Alice on the shingle with lobsters and jellyfish at the water's edge. The washes run to the edges apart from a tiny pale nick on the left at the horizon, which I do not count.

The tea party is right: Hare, Hatter, sleeping Dormouse and a pensive Alice. The card tucked in the Hatter's hat band carries small pseudo-marks and the pocket watch on the table has a marked dial, neither readable.

Soldiers crouch over the garments throwing dice while one holds the clothing, with the crucified Jesus on the hill behind and no blood dwelt on. The board above the cross carries pseudo-script and the dice show pips, both unreadable.

Holmes holds the blue stone up to the window light while Watson stands by the fire with his bag. Lined papers on the desk carry pseudo-writing and the mantel clock has a marked face (unreadable); the open strong box holds several blue gems, an oddity. Holmes's gaunt profile is reminiscent of Peter Cushing but not clearly enough to count.

Holmes kneels on the bed lashing his cane at the bell-pull beneath the ventilator while Watson sits staring. A lit match lies on the bedspread, which is odd but minor; no lettering, and the dark paint reaches every edge.

The prophet stretches his arm over a valley strewn with dry bones, holding a blank tablet and stylus. He is the one told to prophesy, so he belongs in the scene; no figure is made of God and nothing is written.

Small Alice looks up at the Caterpillar on its mushroom with the hookah. The Caterpillar has an old man's human face with a bowler and waistcoat rather than an animal head, breaking the animals-as-animals rule; the top-left corner and top fade to white paper, which this item accepts.

Holmes kneels on the cellar flags with the lantern while Merryweather perches on a crate and Watson stands behind. One lens hangs unheld at Holmes's eye while a second lens is in his hand on the floor, and Merryweather holds two sticks; the washes reach the edges without bare paper.
Jesus stands in the stern with his arm out as the sea flattens, the disciples around him under a torn sail. No lettering, sound hands and paint to every edge.
The grinning Cat sits on a bough showing claws and teeth while Alice stands below with her hands clasped. Nothing is lettered and the paint reaches the edges.

Four soldiers kneel over the garments, one with a cupped hand as if casting. Jesus on the cross behind is still fully dressed in tunic and blue mantle while his clothing is being divided, which contradicts the moment; the board above him is blank, and the left side and corners fade to cream paper, which this item accepts.

The Mock Turtle and Gryphon dance round Alice on the shingle with lobsters, small turtles and jellyfish in the shallows. The pale sky along the top is painted rather than bare, and I see no lettering.
Peter, wrapped in his coat, leaps from the boat into the sea while the beloved disciple points to the figure by a fire on shore and the others haul the full net. Hands and faces are sound.

Holmes thumps the pavement with his stick before the pawnbroker's door under three gilt balls, Watson beside him and the railed weedy square behind. The brown board over the shop carries faded letter strokes that cannot be read. Holmes's profile is reminiscent of Peter Cushing but not clearly enough to count.

Alice faces the Caterpillar on its mushroom with the hookah. The Caterpillar has an old man's human face, bowler and waistcoat with crossed arms rather than an animal head, breaking the animals-as-animals rule; the hookah's ornament is decoration, not writing.
Alice sits in the armchair at the tea table facing the March Hare with his cup, the sleeping Dormouse and a wide-eyed Hatter. The hat carries only a small ochre fleck, no lettering.

A busy courtyard of coin, jars and storehouses being filled suits the verse, and Wisdom is not drawn as a figure. Scribes at right and lower left write scrolls covered in rows of pseudo-script (unreadable); the sky along the top is bare white paper, which this item accepts.
Aged Adam lies dying on bedding in a tent with his family mourning around him and an elder kneeling with hands on him. Hands are sound and nothing is lettered.

Peter grips the seated lame man's right hand and pulls him up, John behind and a crowd at the temple gate. The gate's door-frame carries a band of glyph-like pseudo-inscription (unreadable); the corners and sides fade to white paper, which this item accepts.

Oversized Alice bends in dismay over the upset jury-box of dressed birds and beasts, the Lizard on the floor and the King pointing. Papers on the floor and a juror's sheet carry squiggle lines of pseudo-writing (unreadable); a small extra bewigged judge at the back is not prominent, and the paint reaches the edges.

Alice laughs with the flamingo under her arm as the hedgehog crawls off and the Queen shouts. The left arch soldier has arms and hands at both ends and no legs; courtiers at left and centre are human-bodied men in pip doublets rather than flat cards; the pips on the cards are the only marks.

David stands with sling and bag as the giant topples, the stone at his helmet brow, both armies watching and no blood shown. He falls backward rather than on his face and the lower spear has a blade at each end, both minor.

Samuel pours the horn over kneeling David in a shaft of light, Jesse at left. Among the three brothers at right stands a youth with David's own face and curls carrying a sling and shepherd's bag, so David appears twice; another brother wears Roman-style armour.

The picture is a lone man with a rolled scroll and pen case at his belt gazing up in a village street, with villagers and a Roman soldier small behind. He reads as the letter's author standing in for his own words, a narrator the verse does not call for; the scroll is blank.

The verse is about the pig, and no pig or any animal appears. Instead Moses with his staff and Aaron in the breastplate stand large in the foreground of the camp before the tabernacle; the bright cloud above it holds no figure.
Hezekiah in a gold circlet stands at the carved temple doors while Levites carry in sacks and jars, with the bronze sea on its oxen and the city behind. The door carvings are ornament, not writing.

Seven angels hover in the temple but they are ordinary two-winged angels (one with an extra pair over its face, one hiding its face with its arms); none has six wings or covers its feet, so the visionary creatures do not follow the text. Isaiah stands large in the foreground as the one seeing the vision, which I do not count as extra; the cloud of glory holds no figure.

Holmes with pipe and lens stands looking over the corner pawnbroker's under the three gilt balls, Watson beside him and the railed weedy square behind. A signature-like scrawl is painted in the bottom-right corner on the flagstones; the shop board and wall plaque are blank.

An elder gestures onward with three generations of family behind him and three rolled scrolls on a stone bench, a fair picture of a genealogy. The scrolls are blank and the wash reaches the edges; he could be read as a teller but carries no writer's attributes.

Holmes pulls Watson in by the arm at the door while stout red-haired Wilson sits by the fire. A tobacco tin on the mantel has a label in legible capitals (roughly 'TUGGERS'), with pseudo-script on a second tin, a pinned note and a desk sheet; the right edge breaks to white paper, which this item accepts. A wall light switch is an anachronism, and Holmes's profile is reminiscent of Peter Cushing but not clearly enough to count.

A man with a scroll and pen case at his belt addresses a dozen listeners in a house. He reads as the letter's author speaking his own words, a speaker the verse does not call for; hands are sound and the scroll is blank.
